documents.title: ISSHP International Society for the Study of Hypertension in Pregnancy classification diagnosis and management

chunks.content: Background Preeclampsia (PE) is a hypertensive disorder that occurs during pregnancy, with a reported incidence of 3–8% [ ]. As a major cause of premature birth, PE can threaten both maternal and fetal/neonatal life, accounting for more than 50,000 maternal and 500,000 neonatal deaths annually worldwide [ ]. The detailed and exact etiology of PE remains unknown. However, inadequate trophoblast invasion and angiogenesis, resultant inappropriate remodeling of uterine spiral arteries, and increased production of antiangiogenic factors, such as soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) and soluble endoglin (sEng), have been identified as crucial contributors [ , ]. These inappropriate responses can lead to uteroplacental dysfunction and subsequent maternal endothelial dysfunction, contributing to the development of PE. Uteroplacental dysfunction, which causes placental hypoxic conditions and nutritional deficiency, leads to fetal growth restriction (FGR). Although various studies have investigated treatments for suppressing PE progression [ ], a practical and effective treatment has yet to be identified. Thus, delivery is currently the only treatment option for PE. In 2018, the International Society for the Study of Hypertension in Pregnancy (ISSHP) revised the definitions of PE and categorized PE into three classes: PE with proteinuria (classical criteria), dysfunction of other maternal organs, and uteroplacental dysfunction [ ]. Thus, the initial findings of PE (IFsPE) can vary considerably across patients at the time of diagnosis. Therefore, we hypothesized that evaluating and differentiating clinical features according to each IFsPE through risk classification may enable appropriate IFsPE-based management. However, the impacts and adverse clinical outcomes associated with different IFsPE have not been reported. Thus, our objective is to identify the predictors of pregnancy complications and adverse pregnancy outcomes based on IFsPE according to the new ISSHP criteria. Methods Study design and subjects A retrospective cohort study was designed with approval from the Ethical Committee of Juntendo University Urayasu Hospital (No. 2020–044). The medical records of mothers and neonates were obtained from our electronic medical database. This study included pregnant women who delivered at our teaching hospital between January 2015 and December 2019. Patients with PE were reclassified based on the new ISSHP criteria and divided into three groups based on IFsPE according to the ISSHP classifications: Classification 1 ( C-1 ), proteinuria (classical criteria); Classification 2 ( C-2 ), damage to other maternal organs; and Classification 3 ( C-3 ), uteroplacental dysfunction. As shown in Fig. , all patients were diagnosed with PE under one of three circumstances: (i) IFsPE complicated later by hypertension, (ii) simultaneous onset of IFsPE and hypertension, or (iii) hypertension complicated later by IFsPE. Diagnosis and management of preeclampsia Patients were classified using the new 2018 ISSHP criteria to diagnose PE [ ]. Hypertension was defined as systolic blood pressure > 140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure > 90 mmHg when measured on at least two occasions. According to the new criteria, PE can be diagnosed in the absence of proteinuria (defined as a protein level > 300 mg/day over 24 h or a measured urinary protein to creatinine ratio > 0.3) when maternal organ dysfunction or uteroplacental dysfunction occur. Maternal organ dysfunction includes renal insufficiency, liver involvement with or without right upper quadrant involvement or epigastric abdominal pain, neurological complications (altered mental status, blindness, stroke, clonus, severe headaches, persistent visual scotomata), and hematological complications (platelet counts < 150,000/μL, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemolysis). Uteroplacental dysfunction includes FGR, abnormal umbilical artery (UA) Doppler waveforms, and stillbirth. In ultrasound examinations, the fetal biparietal diameter (BPD) and femur length (FL) were measured using the linear function, and abdominal circumference (AC) was measured using the ellipse function according to the standard techniques outlined by the Japan Society of Ultrasonics in Medicine (JSUM) [ ]. The ultrasonography equipment automatically estimated the fetal weight (EFW) using the formula proposed by the JSUM: EFW (g) = 1.07 × BPD (cm) 3 + 0.30 × AC (cm) 2 × FL (cm). FGR was diagnosed if the EFW was below the 10th percentile for gestational age according to the Japanese fetal growth curve [ ]. Ultrasound examinations and nonstress tests were performed at least once a week. Blood pressure was evaluated at least three times daily, and blood samples were collected at least once a week. Rest was prescribed to the patients, and oral antihypertensive drugs, such as methyldopa, calcium blockers, α- and β-blockers, and intravenous calcium blockers, were administered if necessary. Magnesium sulfate (MgSO 4 ) was administered to patients with eclampsia or high risk of eclampsia to prevent seizures. Initially, 4 g of MgSO 4 was administered intravenously for 30 min, followed by a continued dose of 1 g/h and close monitoring of the serum magnesium level and related side effects. Antenatal betamethasone was administered to mothers to promote fetal lung maturation before 34 weeks of gestation. Delivery was indicated by the inability to control maternal blood pressure using antihypertensive

and oral antihypertensive drugs, such as methyldopa, calcium blockers, α- and β-blockers, and intravenous calcium blockers, were administered if necessary. Magnesium sulfate (MgSO 4 ) was administered to patients with eclampsia or high risk of eclampsia to prevent seizures. Initially, 4 g of MgSO 4 was administered intravenously for 30 min, followed by a continued dose of 1 g/h and close monitoring of the serum magnesium level and related side effects. Antenatal betamethasone was administered to mothers to promote fetal lung maturation before 34 weeks of gestation. Delivery was indicated by the inability to control maternal blood pressure using antihypertensive drugs; placental abruption; eclampsia; hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome; nonreassuring fetal status (NRFS); fetal growth arrest lasting 2 weeks; stillbirth; or 37 weeks of gestation. The attending physician selected the mode of delivery according to obstetric and fetal conditions. To investigate differences in clinical features and maternal/neonatal prognoses among the three groups based on IFsPE ( C-1 , C-2 , and C-3 ), the following items were evaluated and compared: maternal age, pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI), pregnancy history, the indication of delivery (maternal or fetal factors), and gestational age at PE diagnosis. Pregnancy complications, including premature birth at < 37 weeks, FGR, NRFS, and placental abruption, were assessed. Adverse pregnancy outcomes, including acidosis (defined as UA pH < 7.20), Apgar score at 5 min < 7, stillbirth, neonatal mortality, and composite adverse pregnancy outcomes, were recorded. Composite adverse pregnancy outcomes were defined as the presence of one or more of the following conditions: acidosis, Apgar score at 5 min < 7, stillbirth, and neonatal mortality. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 18.0 for Windows (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL). Differences between two groups were evaluated using Student’s t -test for continuous variables and chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests for categorical variables. Differences among three groups were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance with multiple comparisons, followed by a post-hoc Tukey’s test for continuous variables and Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables. The complication risks in each group are presented as crude odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs). P -values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. All data are presented as the mean ± SD or n (%). Results Among 3729 women who delivered at our teaching hospital between January 2015 and December 2019, 158 (4.2%) were diagnosed with PE. After excluding 19 cases of multiple pregnancies, 139 (88.0%) single pregnancy PE cases remained. An additional 35 cases were excluded on the basis of superimposed PE. The remaining 104 (74.8%) cases were included in our analysis (Fig. ). Comparison of pregnancy complications and adverse pregnancy outcomes among C-1, C-2, and C-3 The baseline characteristics of the three groups ( C-1 vs. C-2 vs. C-3 ) are presented and compared in Table . Of 104 subjects, 42 (40.4%), 28 (26.9%), and 34 (32.7%) were classified into the C-1 , C-2 , and C-3 groups, respectively. No significant differences in maternal age, pre-pregnancy BMI (including a BMI > 25 kg/m 2 ), primiparous rate, and indication of delivery were detected among the three groups. However, the gestational age at PE diagnosis was significantly lower in the C-3 group. Pregnancy complications across the three groups are presented and compared in Table . The rate of premature birth at < 37 weeks of gestation was significantly higher in C-3 than in C-1 and C-2 . The temporal relationship between the time of PE diagnosis and delivery is illustrated in Fig. . The percentage of patients with FGR was also significantly higher ( p < 0.0001) in the C-3 group [34 (100.0%)] than in C-1 [7 (16.7%)] and C-2 [4 (14.3%)] groups. No significant differences in the rates of NRFS and placental abruption were detected among groups. Adverse pregnancy outcomes across the three groups are presented and compared in Table . The number of patients with neonatal acidosis was significantly higher in C-3 than in C-1 and C-2 groups. Apgar scores < 7 at 5 min, stillbirth, and neonatal mortality could not be compared among groups due to the small sample sizes; thus, we assessed the composite of these adverse pregnancy outcomes. Significantly more patients in the C-3 group experienced composite adverse pregnancy outcomes compared to those in the other groups. Discussion Our findings demonstrated that patients diagnosed with PE in whom the IFsPE was uteroplacental dysfunction ( C-3 group) had significantly lower gestational ages at delivery and higher rates of FGR, acidosis, and composite adverse pregnancy outcomes than those in the other two groups. Thus, patients classified into the C-3 group showed the most unfavorable prognoses in terms of adverse pregnancy outcomes, indicating that special attention and more careful management are necessary for C-3 PE patients. Discussion Our findings demonstrated that patients diagnosed with PE in whom the IFsPE was uteroplacental dysfunction ( C-3 group) had significantly lower gestational ages at delivery and higher rates of FGR, acidosis, and composite adverse pregnancy outcomes than those in the other two groups. Thus, patients classified into the C-3 group showed the most unfavorable prognoses in terms of adverse pregnancy outcomes, indicating that special attention and more careful management are necessary for C-3 PE patients. We identified the clinical prognostic factors among the three classification groups of patients with PE, which provides useful information for managing PE and explaining the medical condition and associated risks to patients and their families. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to compare pregnancy complications and adverse pregnancy outcomes among the three new ISSHP categories based on IFsPE. However, due to the small sample size, we were unable to classify the IFsPE of maternal organ dysfunction (such as renal insufficiency, liver involvement, neurological complications, and hematological complications) in the C-2 group in detail. Additional case data is needed to compare detailed outcomes and clarify the differences in prognoses across groups to establish guidelines for IFsPE-based management of PE in the future. In 2018, the ISSHP revised its definitions of PE [ ]. In contrast to the ISSHP criteria, the 2013 American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists PE diagnostic criteria do not include uteroplacental dysfunction because it should be managed similarly in patients with or without PE [ ]. FGR is the most common uteroplacental dysfunction, representing all patients in the C-3 group in our cohort. FGR is associated with an increased risk of maternal and neonatal complications in PE patients [ – ]. A previous study revealed that the gestational age at delivery was significantly lower, and the rates of maternal complications and neonatal adverse outcomes were significantly higher in PE patients with FGR than those without FGR [ , ]. In contrast, another study concluded that gestational age at delivery and maternal complication rates were similar among PE patients with and without FGR; however, a higher risk of intrauterine fetal death (a neonatal adverse outcome) was associated with FGR [ ]. Based on these findings, it is unclear whether PE patients with FGR are more likely to experience maternal complications than PE patients without FGR. As uteroplacental dysfunction is a significant etiology of PE, it is an acceptable diagnostic criterion for PE. In addition, Mitani et al. [ ] reported that approximately 15% of patients with FGR experienced proteinuria as a complication, which was diagnosed as PE, suggesting that patients with FGR required close monitoring for PE detection. While the exact etiology of PE remains unclear, a two-stage disorder theory for the etiology and pathology of PE was recently proposed [ , ]. Evidence-based methods of prevention or treatment have not yet been established; therefore, it is clinically important to be aware of early PE-related symptoms or findings, which can widely vary among patients, allowing for appropriate and early management based on risk classification. Our investigation is the first to focus on adverse pregnancy outcomes of PE patients classified according to the new ISSHP criteria based on IFsPE. We compared adverse pregnancy outcomes among C-1 , C-2 , and C-3 groups. Poor prognoses were observed in patients in the C-3 group, including higher risks of lower gestational age at delivery, FGR, and composite adverse pregnancy outcomes in the C-3 group than in the other two groups. In addition, the number of patients with neonatal acidosis was significantly higher in the C-3 group compared to the other groups. These findings indicate that special attention, such as additional gynecological checkup, should be paid when patients are diagnosed with PE based on uteroplacental dysfunction as the IFsPE in the following situations: uteroplacental dysfunction complicated later by hypertension, simultaneous onset of uteroplacental dysfunction and hypertension, and hypertension complicated later by uteroplacental dysfunction. As shown in Table , most PE patients with FGR were diagnosed with PE based on FGR as the IFsPE. However, antiangiogenic factor production might increase with worsening uteroplacental circulation, subsequently inducing FGR and exacerbating maternal endothelial dysfunction. Previous studies have demonstrated that sFlt-1 levels, sEng levels, and the sFlt-1 to placental growth factor (PIGF) ratio (sFlt-1/PIGF) were significantly increased in PE patients with FGR compared to those in patients without FGR [ , ], which supports our conjecture. Further research is required to clarify the relationship between uteroplacental dysfunction and maternal endothelial dysfunction. Moreover, the UA O 2 level was significantly lower in PE patients with FGR than in those without FGR and in PE patients categorized into the C-3 group than those in the C-1 and C-2 groups (Supplementary Table ). Therefore, we

maternal endothelial dysfunction. Previous studies have demonstrated that sFlt-1 levels, sEng levels, and the sFlt-1 to placental growth factor (PIGF) ratio (sFlt-1/PIGF) were significantly increased in PE patients with FGR compared to those in patients without FGR [ , ], which supports our conjecture. Further research is required to clarify the relationship between uteroplacental dysfunction and maternal endothelial dysfunction. Moreover, the UA O 2 level was significantly lower in PE patients with FGR than in those without FGR and in PE patients categorized into the C-3 group than those in the C-1 and C-2 groups (Supplementary Table ). Therefore, we speculated that patients with FGR had underlying chronic fetal hypoxia due to uteroplacental dysfunction, which limited the gas and nutrient exchange and caused the resultant FGR. In recent years, the application of hemoglobin vesicles to treat conditions such as brain ischemia and massive obstetric hemorrhage has been suggested based on the results of animal model experiments [ – ]. Heng Li et al. [ ] demonstrated that artificial nano-oxygen carriers can be used to successfully treat placental hypoxia and manage FGR and apoptotic damage in the brain using a PE rat model. Given our results, this noninvasive therapy could potentially delay the progression of PE and improve neonatal outcomes. However, if lower UA O 2 levels are caused by fetal conditions such as NRFS rather than underlying chronic fetal hypoxia, this treatment option would not be viable. The limitations of this study should be acknowledged. Our results may reflect the differences between gestational age at diagnosis. We understand the necessity of adjustment for gestational age; however, our small sample size did not allow us to perform a multiple logistic regression. Our results, especially the significantly higher rates of pregnancy complications, such as premature birth and FGR, in the C-3 group, may be related to the earlier onset of PE. Regardless, our findings suggest that pregnant women with uteroplacental dysfunction as the IFsPE may require extra attention during pregnancy due to a higher risk for earlier onset of PE. Additionally, this was a single-center retrospective cohort study with a small sample size, which might have affected the results of the study. In particular, the sample sizes of various C-2 group IFsPE types, such as renal insufficiency, liver involvement, neurological complications, and hematological complications, were small; therefore, we could not clarify the differences based on detailed IFsPE. To establish detailed guidelines for the IFsPE-based management of PE, a study with a large sample size is required to verify the accuracy of our results and detect differences in prognoses across the detailed IFsPE groups. Finally, our hospital is a perinatal medical center, and severe PE patients were likely to be transferred, which may result in some differences compared with general hospitals. This is the first study to compare maternal and neonatal prognoses among the three new ISSHP categories based on IFsPE. All data were electronically recorded, and patients were retrospectively reclassified and diagnosed with PE according to the 2018 ISSHP criteria, preventing selection bias. We showed that PE patients presenting with uteroplacental dysfunction as the IFsPE had poor prognoses, especially for outcomes related to perinatal health, such as premature birth, FGR, acidosis, and composite adverse pregnancy outcomes. Our findings suggest that IFsPE may be a predictor of perinatal prognosis. Conclusions In summary, our study suggested that more unfavorable prognoses, including higher risks of premature birth, FGR, acidosis, and composite adverse pregnancy outcomes, were observed in PE patients classified in the C-3 group (presenting with uteroplacental dysfunction as the IFsPE) than in other groups. Thus, special attention and more careful management are necessary for PE patients categorized into the C-3 group. Moreover, careful and close observation, especially in terms of the adverse outcomes related to perinatal health, is required in patients presenting with uteroplacental dysfunction prior to PE diagnosis. Our results are useful in terms of explaining the expected prognosis of PE to patients and their families. Additional studies with larger sample sizes should be conducted to confirm our findings. documents.title: ISSHP Classification Diagnosis Management Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

chunks.content: Background Preeclampsia (PE) affects 2% to 8% of pregnant women and is one of the leading causes of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality [ ]. Worldwide, 76,000 women and 500,000 babies die yearly from this disorder. In France, PE complicates 2,3% of pregnancies [ ]. The only effective treatment to prevent PE is low-dose aspirin [ – ]. Many good quality randomized trials combined in several meta-analyses have shown that treatment with aspirin in women identified as being at risk of PE (according to various definitions) reduces the incidence of PE, prematurity and perinatal mortality [ – ]. The meta-analysis by Askie et al. including over 37,000 patients in 59 trials assessing aspirin in primary and secondary prevention is the only one to be based on individual patient data [ ]. It showed a significant reduction in the risk of PE (RR 0.90; 95% CI 0.84–0.97), in delivery before 34 WG (RR 0.90; 95% CI 0.83–0.98), and in the risk of unfavorable outcomes (RR 0.90; 95% CI 0.85–0.96). The benefit was more marked when aspirin was started before 20 WG and when the dosage was ≥ 75 mg/day. In subgroup analyses, aspirin was not associated with a signification reduction in PE in nulliparas, women with chronic hypertension, women with pregestational diabetes, those aged > 35 years, multifetal pregnancies, and history of a small-for-gestational-age infant. Subsequent meta-analyses, based on aggregate data, and focusing on early aspirin administration at doses of at least 75 mg/day in women at risk according to various definitions, found an even wider beneficial effect of LDA [ – ]. These findings prompted new guidelines that significantly broadened the indications of aspirin for preventing PE in patients considered at risk, according to various combinations of risk factors [ , ]. Several guidelines recommend aspirin for pregnant women with one or more major risk factors for PE, including a history of PE, multifetal gestation, chronic hypertension, pregestational type 1 or 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and autoimmune disorders (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome); and for women with at least two moderate risk factors for PE, including nulliparity, obesity (BMI > 30), a family history of PE (mother or sister), race-ethnicity group, low income, age ≥ 35 years, and some obstetric history events (e.g., low birth weight, previous adverse pregnancy outcomes, > 10-year pregnancy interval, or use of in vitro fertilization) [ , ]. However, how to define the group of pregnant women at risk of PE who would most benefit from aspirin therapy remains unclear. The uncertainty led to diverse guidelines. Based on the Askie et al. meta-analysis’s findings, the French joint guidelines from the national societies of obstetricians (CNGOF) and cardiologists (SFHTA) recommend prescription of aspirin only to women with a history of PE [ , ]. Other countries, such as the USA (ACOG and USPSTF), UK (NICE), Australia and New-Zealand (RANZCOG), and Canada (SOGC), have much broader recommendations, with prescription of aspirin for patients with a least one major risk factor or 2 moderate risk factors, which exposes nearly 30% of pregnant women to aspirin [ , ]. Although maternal and fetal adverse events related to aspirin are rare [ ], the broadening of the indications for aspirin in pregnant women has led to the exposure to these potential side effects of more and more women and fetuses. The ACOG or NICE recommendations would lead each year to the treatment of 5,400,000 in China, 1,200,000 pregnant women in the USA and 240,000 in France [ ]. It therefore appears essential to design and implement screening tools that offer the best benefit-risk balance and limit the needless exposure of pregnant women to aspirin. Beyond, clinical factors alone, in order to better target patients at risk of PE, screening tests have been developed over the past twenty years, integrating clinical parameters, Doppler indices of the uterine arteries and diverse biochemical markers [ – ]. Initially, these tests have had insufficient sensitivity and/or generated a false-positive rate that was too high to be used in clinical practice. The first study that really paved the way for early detection was that published in 2009 by Poon et al. [ ]. The authors proposed the Fetal Medicine Foundation (FMF) algorithm to estimate between 11 and 14 WG the risk of occurrence of PE based on maternal characteristics (age, height, weight, ethnicity, smoking), medical and obstetrical history (chronic hypertension, diabetes, systemic lupus erythematosus, anti-phospholipid syndrome, nulliparity), uterine artery pulsatility index, mean arterial pressure and serum levels of maternal placental growth factor (PlGF) and PAPP-A (if PlGF measurement is not available) [ ]. In the original study, the test identified 91% of early PE, with a false-positive rate of 10%. However, it was not efficient at predicting late PE or gestational hypertension. This case–control analysis presented potential biases, especially in the constitution

to estimate between 11 and 14 WG the risk of occurrence of PE based on maternal characteristics (age, height, weight, ethnicity, smoking), medical and obstetrical history (chronic hypertension, diabetes, systemic lupus erythematosus, anti-phospholipid syndrome, nulliparity), uterine artery pulsatility index, mean arterial pressure and serum levels of maternal placental growth factor (PlGF) and PAPP-A (if PlGF measurement is not available) [ ]. In the original study, the test identified 91% of early PE, with a false-positive rate of 10%. However, it was not efficient at predicting late PE or gestational hypertension. This case–control analysis presented potential biases, especially in the constitution of the control group, which could lead to an overestimation of the performance of the algorithm. Other algorithms were then developed in large prospective cohorts, but their predictive value has proven disappointing [ , ]. The FMF algorithm remains the most studied to date and has been validated in a large population of 35,948 pregnant women in the UK, with an estimated area under the curve of 0.91, sensitivity of 75% for a fixed false-positive rate of 10% for the prediction of early PE [ ]. A major milestone was the multicenter randomized trial ASPRE conducted in the UK to evaluate the benefit of treatment with aspirin versus placebo in primary prevention of PE in patients considered at risk, based on the FMF algorithm [ ]. Eligible patients were those with a predicted risk of PE > 1/100. Those who agreed to participate were randomized to receive either aspirin (150 mg per day) or placebo. Treatment was started in the first trimester (between 11 and 14 WG) and continued until 36 WG. The screening offered to 26,941 pregnant women made it possible to select 2,641 patients estimated to be at high risk for PE. Of these, 1776 patients were randomized for treatment with aspirin or placebo. This trial showed a reduction in the level of PE with delivery before 37 WG (primary endpoint), which occurred in 13/798 patients (1.6%) in the aspirin group versus 35/822 patients (4.3%) in the placebo group (OR 0.38; 95% CI 0.20–0.74; p = 0.004), but no reduction in the overall rate of PE. No significant difference was found in the incidence of PE after 37 weeks (OR 0.95 95% CI 0.57–1.57). A non-significant reduction in perinatal mortality was reported (OR 0.59 95% CI 0.19—1.85). The trial was not calibrated to have sufficient power to show a possible difference in severe maternal and perinatal morbidity, including adverse effects of aspirin. In total, in the ASPRE study, the screening procedure had to be applied to almost 27,000 women to obtain a reduction of 23 cases of PE with delivery before 37 WG, with no demonstrated effect on the overall health of women and children between the placebo and aspirin groups. The ASPRE study is important but does not allow to demonstrate the benefit of implementing universal screening for PE in the general population. It does not show a reduction in the overall rate of PE and, above all, does not show any benefit in terms of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. Indeed, reducing the incidence of PE cannot be considered a sufficient endpoint if this reduction is not associated with a demonstrated improvement in the health for mother and child. Furthermore, the impact of this universal screening in terms of healthcare consumption, iatrogenic risks, psychological impact and costs, in particular for patients considered at risk but not developing PE (false positives from screening) has not been assessed. To consider implementing screening for PE in the general population of pregnant women, it is then essential to demonstrate its benefits on robust health outcomes and not only on the PE diagnosis, as well as to assess its potential adverse consequences and costs. This evaluation is all the more crucial since while this screening is not recommended by most of the national guidelines, it is currently offered to an increasing number of women. The objective of the RANSPRE trial is to study the impact on perinatal and maternal health outcomes of first trimester PE screening associated with aspirin treatment of pregnant women screened at risk. A medical-economic evaluation allowing a cost-effectiveness analysis will be carried out. The results of this study will constitute essential information that will guide policymaking for the prevention of PE in the general population of pregnant women. Participants Inclusion criteria Pregnancy between 11 and 14 WG Age ≥ 18 years Affiliated to or beneficiary of a health insurance system Signed informed consent Exclusion criteria Gestational age <11 WG or > 14 WG Known ectopic pregnancy Known

Methods and analysis Design of the study RANSPRE is a multicenter randomized controlled open-label trial with 2 parallel groups (ratio 1:1), with or without screening for PE in the first trimester of pregnancy. Setting Twenty-two maternity hospitals in France. Participants Inclusion criteria Pregnancy between 11 and 14 WG Age ≥ 18 years Affiliated to or beneficiary of a health insurance system Signed informed consent Exclusion criteria Gestational age <11 WG or > 14 WG Known ectopic pregnancy Known non-ongoing pregnancy Known multiple pregnancy History of PE in a previous pregnancy Pregnancies complicated by major fetal abnormality identified at the 1 st trimester ultrasound if performed before randomization Absence of health insurance Contra-indication to aspirin (bleeding disorders such as Von Willebrand’s disease, active peptic ulceration, hypersensitivity to aspirin, NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease, severe liver or heart dysfunction) Women taking low-dose (75–160 mg/day) aspirin regularly before pregnancy (except ART indication) Age<18 years Poor understanding of the French language Eligible women will be identified early in pregnancy at their first prenatal visit in the maternity hospital, before or at the time of the first-trimester ultrasound, and will be referred to the research midwife to be fully informed on and participate in the study. Women agreeing to participate in the RANSPRE trial will be randomized either to the experimental group or to the control group. Randomization The randomization list will be created by an independent statistician prior to the start of the research project. The numbers of participants in the two groups will be balanced, with a 1:1 ratio, and variable block size. Randomization will be stratified by center and parity (in 2 categories, nulliparous yes or no) (as mentioned in the state-of-the-art section, nulliparity is a major risk factor for PE). A confidential document describing the preparation of the randomization list will be kept in the Department of Biostatistics and Methodology (CIC Mère-Enfant, Cochin Hospital, Paris). A validated web-based system will be used to implement random assignment to each group. Interventions Patients included in the study RANSPRE will be randomized in one of the two following groups (Fig. ): Group A: experimental group Women randomized to the experimental group with first-trimester PE screening (group A) will have usual first-trimester ultrasound with the addition of Doppler study of the uterine arteries, a blood pressure measurement according to the FMF protocol and a blood test to quantify serum PlGF concentration. PlGF serum concentration will be assessed using IVDR-certified, commercially available immunoassay platforms (Revvity, Thermo Fisher Scientific and Roche Diagnostics) in the hospital laboratory. The individual risk of developing preeclampsia before 37 weeks’ gestation is calculated by the dedicated software integrating clinical parameters and PlGF concentration. The risk result will be available within 24 h after sampling and within 5 days after randomization. o For women with a positive screening test (group A1, estimated risk > 1/100), a treatment with aspirin will be prescribed at 160 mg/day once a day at dinner, started as soon as possible and before 15 WG, and taken up to 36 WG. o For women with negative screening (group A2, estimated risk ≤ 1/100), usual pregnancy follow-up without aspirin treatment will be offered. Group B: control group Women randomized to the group without first-trimester PE screening (group B) will have first-trimester ultrasound without Doppler study of the uterine arteries. Serum PlGF concentration will not be assessed. Usual pregnancy follow-up without aspirin treatment will be offered. Follow-up For patients of group A1, a phone interview will be performed by the midwife or the investigator of the center two weeks after treatment initiation in order to verify treatment observance and to collect potential side-effects related to aspirin. If the patient has not initiated aspirin a second phone call will be done 1 week after. Prenatal care will be performed at the participating maternity hospital for them (group A1). At week 28 (± 2 weeks), a specific visit with the research midwife will be planned at the same time of the routine visit. In case this 28WG visit cannot be performed at the maternity a phone interview with the midwife will be planed. Patients treated by aspirin and experiencing epigastric pain will receive anti-acid drugs. In case of bleeding complications, aspirin therapy will be discontinued, as routine practice. The research midwife will also check the patient’s notebook. Patients will continue the routine follow-up of their pregnancy with routine consultations at the maternity hospital, ultrasound examinations and blood tests. The midwife or the doctor in charge of the patient will decide the frequency of these examinations. For all patients, 2 self-administered questionnaires will be filled in. Patients treated by aspirin and experiencing epigastric pain will receive anti-acid drugs. In case of bleeding complications, aspirin therapy will be discontinued, as routine practice. The research midwife will also check the patient’s notebook. Patients will continue the routine follow-up of their pregnancy with routine consultations at the maternity hospital, ultrasound examinations and blood tests. The midwife or the doctor in charge of the patient will decide the frequency of these examinations. For all patients, 2 self-administered questionnaires will be filled in. The first one will be sent electronically at 20 WG (± 2 weeks) and will include the state anxiety items of the State-Anxiety inventory (STAI) [ , ] and the Pregnancy Related Anxiety Questionnaire (PRAQ-R2) [ , ], both validated in French, and questions about perception of information received (all patients) and of screening (group A patients). The second questionnaire will be given during the delivery stay or sent within 30 days post-partum to all patients and will include the state anxiety items of the STAI. Sample size calculation The prevalence of the primary outcome in the general population of pregnant women in France is estimated at 4% (prematurity < 34WG (2.4%) or perinatal mortality (0.7%) or birth weight < 3°P (3%); National Perinatal Survey (ENP) 2016 data). The frequency of the primary outcome among women at risk in the absence of treatment is estimated at 20%, based on the available literature [ , , ]. These women are expected to represent 10% of the general population of pregnant women, as found in populations where the FMF test was applied [ ]. We hypothesize a 50% reduction in the primary outcome in at-risk women treated with aspirin. This hypothesis of reduction is consistent with the 50% reduction in perinatal mortality and prematurity reported in a meta-analysis synthesizing the impact of aspirin given from the first trimester and at a dosage of 100 mg/day or more, in at-risk populations [ ]. The prevalence of the primary outcome is therefore expected to be 10% among women screened at risk in the intervention group versus 20% in at risk women (but not known to be at risk) in the control group. Since these at-risk women are expected to represent 10% of the total population in each group, this leads to an expected 3% prevalence of the primary outcome in the intervention group as a whole versus 4% in the control group. With these assumptions, an alpha risk of 5%, and a power of 90%, the total number of women to be randomized is 14,192. In total, accounting for a 2% lost to follow up rate, it is planned to include 14,500 women. Data collection All patients participating to the study will have signed a consent form allowing the collection of their data and the data of their infant until discharge from hospital. All the information required by the protocol will be recorded in CRFs and an explanation will be provided for any missing data. Data regarding the inclusion criteria in all women, as well as the clinical, biological, and ultrasound parameters of the first trimester PE screening test in women randomized in the intervention arm, will be collected and recorded in the CRF at baseline. Data regarding the women’s satisfaction and anxiety will be collected through self-questionnaires filled in at 20 WG and during the postpartum period, in all women and recorded in the eCRF. Data regarding adherence to aspirin treatment and potential adverse effects will be collected through a phone interview 2 weeks after treatment initiation and a physical interview at the 28 WG prenatal visit, as well as through the content of the aspirin notebook at the end of pregnancy, in women randomized in the intervention arm and who were expected to take aspirin. All other data on the characteristics of the woman and her pregnancy and delivery, and maternal and infant outcomes will be collected from a review of medical records. The data concerning newborns will essentially be those collected at delivery. For the small subgroup of children who will be hospitalized in neonatology, these birth data will be supplemented by those relating to this hospitalization, collected from the child's medical file. No additional data will be collected. Similarly, no intervention will be carried out on the child within the framework of the RANSPRE study. The father of the infant will be informed about the collection of routine medical data during hospitalization for the purpose of the study. A non-opposition of the father will allow the collection of these infant’s data. Statistical analysis An intention-to-treat analysis will be performed as the principal analysis, i.e. all randomized patients will be included in the analysis in the group in which they first were randomized and all their data will be used, regardless of any changes in treatment over the study duration. Multiple imputations will be used to replace missing data for primary outcome. Then a “per protocol analysis” will be performed, in which participants will be included based on the intervention they received. Descriptive analyses will be overall and by group. Qualitative variables will be described by numbers and percentage. Quantitative variables will be described by numbers, mean standard deviation, median, range, 1 st and 3rd quartiles. Comparative analyses between groups for primary and secondary outcomes will be performed with adjustment for stratification factors of randomization (center and parity). Qualitative variables will be compared using the Chi-square test, the corrected Chi-square test, or the exact Fisher test according to the expected values under the hypothesis of independence. To adjust on factors, a logistic or multinomial regression model will be used. The conditions of validity of these models will be checked (log-linearity). Quantitative variables will be compared using the Student t-test if the conditions of validity are respected (normal distribution, homogeneous variances). If the variances are different between both groups, the Student t-test for unequal variances will be used. In the event of non-normal distribution, the Mann–Whitney-Wilcoxon test will be used. To adjust on factors, a linear regression model will be used. The conditions of validity of this model will be checked (normality and homoscedasticity of residuals). Comparisons will be performed with a type I error of 5% for the primary outcome, and adjusted for multiple testing for the secondary outcomes with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, to control the False Discovery Rate at 0.05 [ ]. Given the many secondary endpoints analyzed and to avoid inflation of the type I error risk due to multiple comparisons, we will prespecify endpoints for which a statistical comparison will be conducted and those for which only the association estimate and its 95% CI will be reported. No intermediate analysis is planned. Economic evaluation The economic evaluation comprises a calculation of the costs of tests and treatments, the total pregnancy costs and a cost effectiveness using severe perinatal morbidity as defined by the primary composite criterion as an effectiveness criterion. The short duration of the study and the relative insensitivity of the EQ5D5L quality of life instrument precludes a full cost utility analysis. This is a single trial based economic evaluation, data on hospital resource use will be collected prospectively at the patient level. All patients included in the trial are eligible for the economic evaluation. Analysis of the costs and outcomes for the economic evaluation will follow the intent to treat principle. The analysis is undertaken from the viewpoint of the healthcare system, over a time horizon of 7 months (time between inclusion and delivery) without discounting. Estimating resources and costs Resources of interest comprise all tests, regardless of the setting where they are performed, consultations and tests for the initiation and monitoring of treatments (the aspirin costs are negligible) hospital admissions, transportation in relation to treatment monitoring or admissions and out of pocket costs. The total number and type of consultations, laboratory workup and imaging will be recorded prospectively on the study CRF. Hospital admissions related to the management of the pregnancy from the time of inclusion to the delivery will be recorded and the hospitals ‘database will be queried to extract the full discharge summaries. For transportation, we will record the number of consultations and assume that each required a transportation covered by the social health insurance. The cost of the PE screening test comprises the cost of US and biology required by the algorithm and the cost of the device itself. While the former are listed on the Social Health Insurance schedule, the latter will be estimated from manufacturer’s information provided and subjected to a sensitivity analysis. For hospital costs we will estimate a cost for each admission based upon the DRG cost calculated in the national cost study and adjusted or the actual patients’ length of stay. For the delivery admission, both the mother and the infant’s costs will be calculated and aggregated. We will calculate a total cost for the screening workup and a total medical cost for the pregnancy including the hospital costs of delivery. Out of pocket costs, which should be small given the eligibility for 100% coverage at the 6th month of pregnancy will also be cumulated over the duration of the follow up period. Costs will be presented as means and standard deviations with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals and compared with non parametric tests. Outcomes The outcome for the economic evaluation is the incremental cost effectiveness ratio defined as the difference in total costs divided by the reduction in severe morbidity between the two arms. In order to represent the variability of the joint distribution of costs and outcomes, we will perform nonparametric bootstrapping with 1,000 resamples on the entire population and the result of the bootstrap replications will be presented on the cost effectiveness plane. We will also present the acceptability curve. While results of costs effectiveness analyses are usually expressed in terms of cost/QALY, there are benchmarks for the societal willingness to pay in order to avoid severe neonatal morbidity, with ratios about 15–20,000€ to avoid one adverse event (liveborn with CT, fetal loss, neonatal death or pregnancy termination) in France [ ]. A deterministic sensitivity analysis will use scenarios on the cost of screening. Discussion Potential and implementation of the findings PE affects between 2 and 8% of pregnant women, making it one of the leading causes of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. Apart from delivering the baby and removing the placenta, no other effective curative interventions have yet been demonstrated. Therefore, prevention remains the most effective strategy for reducing the burden of PE. Low-dose aspirin (100—160 mg/day) started before 20 WG reduces the incidence of PE, prematurity, perinatal mortality and low birth weight. However important controversy remains concerning the indications of aspirin to prevent PE, particularly which group of pregnant women at risk of PE would most benefit from aspirin therapy. Many guidelines recommend aspirin for pregnant women with one or more high-risk factors, or with at least two moderate-risk factors for PE. These recommendations would result in the treatment of 240,000 pregnant women in France, 1.2 million in the USA and 5.4 million in China each year. Adverse events related to aspirin use in pregnant women and their fetuses are rare but have been confirmed in nation-wide studies. Therefore, the broadening of the indications for aspirin in pregnant women means that more and more women and fetuses are exposed to these potential side effects. It is therefore essential to implement screening tools that minimize unnecessary exposure of pregnant women to aspirin. To better target patients at risk of PE, screening tests have been developed that integrate clinical parameters, Doppler indices of the uterine arteries, and biochemical markers. The FMF algorithm is the most widely studied to date and has been validated in large populations. The ASPRE study has confirmed that low-dose aspirin is effective in patients identified as high-risk by the FMF algorithm. In order to consider implementing PE screening in the general population, it is essential to demonstrate its benefits in terms of robust health outcomes, not just PE diagnosis, as well as assessing its potential adverse consequences and costs.
